title: Re-running a failed check cannot pick up a fix to the branch it was run against
body:
## What goes wrong

When a proposed change fails its automatic checks because of a defect in the *accepted*
branch rather than in the proposal, the obvious response is to fix the accepted branch and
then re-run the check. This can never work, and the reason is not discoverable from
anything the interface shows you.

Re-running replays the original run. It re-uses the workflow definition, the merge
commit and the state of the accepted branch as they were when the run was first created.
A fix merged afterwards is invisible to it, however many times it is re-run. The only
thing that produces a run which sees the corrected branch is a *new commit on the
proposal* -- pressing "Update branch", or merging the accepted branch in by hand.

What makes this worse than a harmless no-op is that the re-run produces a fresh,
current-looking failure with a plausible and entirely obsolete error message. The reader
concludes the problem is still live and begins investigating something that was fixed
hours earlier. Two people did exactly that here, independently, and one of them had
already diagnosed and fixed the underlying bug himself.

The tell, when it happened, was the *name* of the failing step. The corrected workflow had
renamed that step; the failing run still showed the old name. Nothing else in the output
distinguished the replay from a current run.

How to tell which you are looking at: the check summary on the proposal's own page always
reflects its current head commit, whereas an individual run opened from the list of all
runs may belong to any earlier commit. The proposal's own "mergeable" state is the summary
to trust. Opening a specific historical run and re-running it is the trap.
author: danny
what_was_tried:
A proposal's checks failed because the accepted branch contained a defect in its test
suite -- a test that silently depended on a configured git identity, which the machine
running the checks does not have.

The advice given at the time, by me, was: merge the fixing proposal, then re-run the
failed check. This was stated confidently and was wrong.

Four re-runs followed, all failing identically. The fix was verifiably on the accepted
branch: its checks were passing there. The discrepancy was only resolved by comparing the
name of the failing step against the names in the corrected workflow file, which showed
the run was still executing the old definition.

Pressing "Update branch", which creates a merge commit on the proposal, produced a new run
that passed on the first attempt.

Afterwards a second person, reviewing the proposal, opened the old failed run from the list
of all runs and re-ran it once more, obtaining the same failure and the same obsolete
message, and reasonably concluded that the problem was unresolved.
